title: IT Infrastructure Fundamentals
subject: IT INFRA
description: The building blocks of a business IT environment, the on-premise, cloud, and hybrid choices, and how endpoint and infrastructure deals are shaped by lifecycle and support.

lessons.title: Components of an IT infrastructure
lessons.body:
IT infrastructure is the set of hardware, software, and services that let an organisation run its applications. The main components are:

- **Compute:** servers and desktops or laptops that run applications.
- **Storage:** where data is kept (covered in the Server and Storage course).
- **Network:** switches, routers, and wireless access that connect everything (see Networking Fundamentals).
- **Power and cooling:** UPS units and air conditioning that keep equipment running.
- **Management and security:** monitoring tools, backup, and access control.

A weak link in any of these affects the whole business, so a sound design considers them together.

lessons.title: On-premise, cloud, and hybrid
lessons.body:
Organisations choose where to run workloads:

- **On-premise:** equipment owned and housed by the company. Full control, but the company carries capital cost and upkeep.
- **Cloud:** services rented from a provider. Flexible and quick to scale, with running costs that depend on usage.
- **Hybrid:** a mix, for example core systems on-premise and collaboration tools in the cloud.

The right choice depends on data rules, latency needs, budget pattern, and the skills available in-house. Ask these questions before recommending a model.

lessons.title: The infrastructure lifecycle
lessons.body:
Infrastructure has a lifecycle: planning, procurement, deployment, support, and refresh. Each stage creates a sales opportunity:

- **Planning:** a site survey or capacity review.
- **Procurement:** the right product, warranty, and delivery schedule.
- **Deployment:** installation, configuration, and testing.
- **Support:** service contracts and response times.
- **Refresh:** replacing equipment before it fails or falls out of support.

A customer who has a support contract and a refresh plan is easier to serve and renew than one who buys hardware only once.

lessons.title: Service levels and warranty basics
lessons.body:
A service level agreement (SLA) defines what the supplier promises: response time, resolution time, and uptime. Warranty covers defects within a stated period. Support contracts, such as annual maintenance contracts (AMC), extend or replace warranty cover.

When discussing these terms, state exactly what is covered, what is excluded, and how the customer raises a request. Vague promises create disputes later.
